extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, advanced students, and readers interested in analytic number theory and Waring's problem
extracted.subtask_description: An expository inaugural lecture presenting the formulation and history of additive problems in number theory (partitions, sums of k-th powers), definitions of g(k) and G(k), classical results, existence proofs (Hilbert, Liouville, Maillet, Wieferich, Landau), and the Hardy–Littlewood circle-method approach including the singular series and asymptotic formulae. Also discusses conditional applications (e.g., Goldbach under RH) and computational evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: General additive-problem formulation and r(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose that n is a positive integer and the a's are positive integers of some special kind (squares, cubes, k-th powers, primes, etc.). Consider all expressions n = a1 + a2 + ... + as (with s fixed or unrestricted, a's possibly repeated, order possibly relevant or not). Denote by r(n) the number of representations satisfying the problem's conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the general counting function r(n); clarifies that whether order and repetition are allowed must be stated for each problem. Example: trivial case with a in {1,2,3} gives r(n) as number of solutions of n = x + 2y + 3z in nonnegative integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function / power-series method for additive problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use generating functions (power series) whose coefficients are the representation-counting function r(n). The coefficient of x^n in the product/formulaic generating function equals r(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical extraction of coefficients via algebraic expansion, partial fractions, and Cauchy's theorem; leads to integral representations for r(n) and motivates the circle-method decomposition of the contour integrals. Examples include rational generating functions for finite-support problems and Euler's infinite product for partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between additive and multiplicative theories (choice of analytic tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additive problems are naturally attacked via power series (generating functions), while multiplicative problems (e.g., functions built from prime factorization) are more naturally treated by Dirichlet series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by d(n), the divisor function: its Lambert series (power-series form) is less fundamental than its Dirichlet series (zeta(s)^2). This distinction motivates selecting appropriate analytic machinery for different number-theory problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitions p(n) and Euler's generating function; asymptotics
rubrics_metrics.description: When the a's are all positive integers with repetitions allowed and order irrelevant, r(n) = p(n) (the unrestricted partition function). Euler's generating function is the infinite product Π_{m≥1} (1 − x^m)^{-1}. This function is an elliptic modular function with the unit circle a continuous line of singularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy and Ramanujan's approximate formula (leading asymptotic term described in lecture) gives highly accurate approximations to p(n); numerical comparison with computation (e.g., p(200) to many digits) demonstrates the formula's precision. Analytic difficulties arise from the unit circle being a natural boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of g(k) (Waring's g-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: g(k) is the least positive integer m (if it exists) such that every positive integer n can be expressed as the sum of at most m k-th powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: g(2) = 4 (Lagrange). Waring originally conjectured values (e.g., 9 for cubes), and existence/upper-bounds for g(k) have been established in many cases by explicit identities and constructions (Liouville, Maillet, Wieferich, Hilbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of G(k) (asymptotic / almost-everywhere version)
rubrics_metrics.description: G(k) is the least positive integer m such that every sufficiently large integer (i.e., 'every member from a certain point onwards') is the sum of at most m k-th powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G(k) ≤ g(k), and existence of either implies existence of the other with trivial bounds. G(k) is often the more fundamental quantity for analytic methods (e.g., Landau's theorem gives G(3) < 8 whereas g(3) = 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical results for sums of squares and small-k cases (criteria for representability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterizations and theorems: a number is a sum of two squares iff it has prime factorization of the special form (primes 4m+3 occur to even exponent etc.); a number is a sum of three squares unless it is of the form 4^a(8b+7); Lagrange: every positive integer is a sum of four squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also quantitative results: number of sums-of-two-squares ≤ x is about C x / sqrt(log x) (Landau). For small even s (<10) representations can often be expressed in closed form via divisor sums; for odd s = 3,5,7 there are formulas involving finite quadratic-residue sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs and explicit upper bounds for g(k) via algebraic identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive existence proofs show every integer is a sum of some bounded number of k-th powers by algebraic identities combining lower-power representations (e.g., Liouville's identity for biquadrates leading to finite upper bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liouville showed g(4) exists with an initial bound of 53 later reduced to 37; Maillet, Wieferich and others reduced bounds for cubes leading to exact g(3)=9. Such arguments often combine Lagrange's theorem with algebraic decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landau's finiteness theorem and significance for G(k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Landau proved that the number of integers requiring the maximal number of cubes (9 in classical work) is finite, establishing that many 'extreme' cases are exceptional and suggesting a smaller G(k) than g(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landau's proof used deep results on the asymptotic distribution of primes (transcendental methods). This motivates distinguishing between g(k) (worst-case over all n) and G(k) (eventual behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's theorem (existence of g(k) for all k) and algebraic proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert proved Waring's conjecture (existence of g(k) for every k). Later simplifications (Stridsberg, others) eliminated transcendental parts, giving purely algebraic/elementary existence proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's original method has two parts: an analytic/combinatorial construction of identities for many k (especially powers of 2) and an algebraic extension to all k; these are existence proofs and do not determine exact g(k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardy–Littlewood circle method: major arcs (rational points) vs minor arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose the unit-circle contour integral into contributions from neighborhoods of rational points x = e^{2πip/q} (major arcs) and the rest (minor arcs). The rational points (small q) give dominant, tractable contributions; the remainder must be bounded as an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major arcs correspond to 'lights' of varying intensity (brightest when q smallest). The method builds auxiliary functions fp,q(x) approximating local behavior near each rational point, sums their contributions, and hopes the sum (singular series) approximates the coefficient. Controlling minor arcs is the principal difficulty, especially for k>2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular series and final asymptotic formula for number of representations
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of representations r_s(n) has a main term expressed as a product of a singular series (sum over q of arithmetic exponential sums) and a multiplicative factor ~ constant * n^{s/k - 1}, plus an error term O(n^{s/k - 1 - δ}). The singular series is essentially the sum over q of q^{-s} times Gauss-type exponential sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the singular series is positive and the remainder/error term is of lower order than the main term (which holds when s exceeds a certain threshold), then r_s(n) > 0 for all sufficiently large n, yielding existence of G(k) ≤ s. The singular series often converges quickly and is oscillatory; only a few terms are typically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for proving G(k) (sufficient conditions via the circle method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove G(k) ≤ s, one must obtain an asymptotic formula for r_s(n) whose main term is positive and whose error term is of strictly lower order for large n, so that for sufficiently large n the main term dominates and r_s(n) > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires (a) precise evaluation/control of the singular series (positivity) and (b) sufficiently strong bounds on the minor-arc contributions to make the error smaller than the main term. The lecture gives numerical upper bounds for G(k) obtained this way for many k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and characteristic difficulties for k > 2
rubrics_metrics.description: When k > 2, the major-arc 'beams' (neighborhoods where rational points dominate) are too narrow to cover the contour uniformly; significant parts of the circle remain 'in darkness' (hard-to-control minor arcs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central obstacle that delayed progress; it necessitated introducing the singular series and additional sources of analytic control (e.g., new estimates for exponential sums, finer decomposition) to handle minor arcs and obtain asymptotic formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computation and empirical tables as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale computations (tables by Dase, von Sterneck, Ruckle, MacMahon, etc.) provide empirical distributions of the minimal number of k-th powers required for integers up to large cutoffs and can suggest conjectures about values like G(3) or g(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy discusses interpreting such tables cautiously: empirical disappearance of numbers needing many terms is suggestive (e.g., for cubes, data up to 1,000,000 show 6-cube numbers almost gone), but not a proof. Computation can guide conjectures and test formulae/approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications to Goldbach-type problems under hypotheses (conditional results)
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle-method framework can be adapted to additive-prime problems. Under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (a strong form of the Riemann hypothesis for L-functions), one can prove results such as: every sufficiently large odd integer is the sum of three odd primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a full solution of Goldbach's conjecture but demonstrates the method's potential conditional on deep hypotheses about zeros of zeta/L-functions; it shows how analytic bounds on exponential sums and zero-distribution translate to additive-prime results.
